name: Onion juice
lead: Onion juice is the liquid pressed from the bulb of the common onion (Allium cepa), applied to the scalp as a folk remedy for hair loss and to encourage hair growth. It is discussed in reviews of social-media hair-loss advice alongside rosemary oil, rice water and garlic gel.[1][2]

The best-known clinical evidence is a small 2002 controlled trial in patchy alopecia areata, in which participants applying crude onion juice twice daily for two months were reported to show more regrowth than those applying tap water.[3] Narrative reviews describe the wider literature as limited by small samples, lack of comparison with standard treatments, and conflicts of interest, and note that onion juice has mostly been studied in combination products.[4][5] A 2025 review of online alopecia misinformation lists onion juice among the unproven natural remedies promoted online.[6]

paras: In hair-care communities onion juice is applied to the scalp with the aim of promoting regrowth, thickening or reducing shedding. Reviews of herbal and topical hair products identify it as one of several popular plant-derived actives, together with rosemary oil, saw palmetto and pumpkin seed oil.[4][5]

A 2002 controlled trial in patchy alopecia areata compared crude onion juice (23 patients) with tap water (15 patients) applied twice daily for two months. The authors reported regrowth of coarse terminal hair beginning at about two weeks, in 73.9% of the onion juice group at four weeks and 86.9% at six weeks, versus 13% of the water group at eight weeks.[3] It was a small, single-report study, and reviews note that the broader literature on topical botanicals tends to have small samples, nonuniform groups, and undisclosed alopecia types.[4]

A 2025 review of herbal remedies for hair loss includes onion juice among agents that studies suggest may promote hair growth, while calling for more rigorous evidence.[5] A review of TikTok hair-loss remedies examined the evidence behind onion juice, rosemary oil, rice water and garlic gel.[1] Other human trials of onion juice found in searches concern drinking it (for example, effects on bone markers or cholesterol) and do not address hair.[7][8]
Beyond hair, onion juice has been studied in laboratory and animal work, for example on platelet aggregation in dogs and on experimental cataract in rats, none of which bears on hair growth.[9][10]

Onion juice features in reviews of social-media-driven hair-loss advice. Authors of one review describe sponsored marketing and social platforms as drivers of interest in hair serums and oils,[4] and a qualitative review of online alopecia information lists onion juice among natural remedies it characterises as lacking support.[6]

timeline.event: Controlled trial of crude onion juice versus tap water in alopecia areata published.[3]
Review of TikTok topical hair-loss remedies, including onion juice, published.[1]
Reviews of herbal and topical hair-growth actives and of online alopecia misinformation list onion juice.[4][5][6]

lore.intro: Onion juice appears in social-media hair-loss advice as a natural alternative to conventional treatments.[1][6]

claims.claim: Applying onion juice to the scalp regrows hair
claims.believers: Promoters of natural remedies point to the 2002 alopecia areata trial and to traditional use as support for regrowth claims.[3]
claims.experts: Reviews describe the evidence as limited by small samples and design problems, and a misinformation review lists it as an unproven online remedy.[4][6]

claims.claim: Onion juice can replace conventional hair-loss treatments such as minoxidil or finasteride
claims.believers: Proponents of natural remedies promote them as gentler alternatives.[5]
claims.experts: Reviews note the studies lack comparison with standard therapies and suggest such topicals might serve as add-ons or alternatives only for patients not using conventional options.[4]

card.summary: A folk scalp remedy with one small alopecia areata trial behind it and reviews calling the evidence limited.
card.note: Evidence is a single small 2002 trial plus reviews noting design limits; no large trials.

quick.overview:
Onion juice is pressed from onion bulbs and applied to the scalp as a natural hair-regrowth remedy. It circulates in social-media hair-loss advice alongside rosemary oil and rice water.

A 2002 controlled trial in alopecia areata reported more regrowth than tap water. Reviews describe the evidence base as small and limited.
quick.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms in the literature are not established for onion juice specifically; reviews of herbal remedies cite ideas such as antioxidant effects and improved circulation as general explanations.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed report no specific safety data for scalp use. It is an unregulated food-derived preparation, and reviews advise further study.
